title: N.L. apologizes, says it now accepts Innu history dates back more than 300 years
summary: The Grand Chief of the Innu Nation says Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham has apologized following a months-long controversy over the Innu's history in Labrador.

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
The Grand Chief of the Innu Nation says Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham has apologized following a months-long controversy over the Innu's history in Labrador.
Letter from Premier Tony Wakeham follows months of controversy
Innu Grand Chief emotional after N.L. premier accepts Innu timeline

"Newfoundland and Labrador accepts the position that the history of the Innu in Labrador goes back to the time of immemorial, prior to the arrival of Europeans," Jodie Ashini said on a Facebook livestream Thursday.
Ashini was reading a letter written to her by Wakeham dated Thursday.

Months after delay and ‘long, hard, painful’ path, Innu history exhibit opens in Labrador

blocks.text: The controversy has been making headlines since June, and boiled over when it was revealed that, according to the Innu, the province's archaelogy office only considered the history of the Innu to go back 300 years — which Ashini has called "a theory."

The tension between Ashini and Wakeham boiled over in September, when Ashini walked out of a meeting with Wakeham and later committed that the Innu Nation would not vote to support the new Churchill River deal with Quebec unless the province changed its tune on the Innu's history.
The pair held a nearly three-hour meeting earlier this month. Wakeham had previously committed to an independent audit of Innu records held by the archaeology office.

“I regret the length of time the controversy around the 300-year issue has taken to resolve. I apologize for the problems which arose from the province's position," Wakeham's letter, shared with CBC News, said.
Why is the Innu Nation upset with the N.L. government?
Speaking with reporters late Thursday afternoon, Wakeham said he had an emotional conversation with Ashini on Wednesday.
"To be brutally honest, it was emotional for both of us," Wakeham said.
"It caused me a lot of grief … trying to get to the bottom and understand all of it. And yeah, it was a lot of grief, I think, especially for the Innu Nation."
Federal clarification was what N.L. needed to hear: Wakeham
Wakeham was hesitant to take a stance on the timeline in the months during the dispute, often saying he wanted to wait to get the facts before making a judgment.
On Thursday, Wakeham told reporters he got those facts in October.

As part of land claim negotiations between the Innu, the provincial government and the federal government — which have been ongoing since 1977 — Wakeham said the federal government clarified that Innu have history in Labrador since time immemorial.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says the federal government clarifying to the province that the Innu have been in Labrador since time immemorial was what he needed to be able to move forward in addressing the wrongs felt by the Innu Nation. (Terry Roberts/CBC)
Following that clarification, Wakeham said he felt comfortable to move forward.

"Clearly, I don't see as a province how Newfoundland and Labrador cannot be on the same side as the federal government in acknowledging the Innu. And I spoke to the Grand Chief about that," Wakeham said.
"[I] apologized for the length of time that it had taken and regret the grief that it had caused the Innu Nation.”
Ashini wiped away tears several times throughout the livestream, expressing thanks for the support from "every single Innu."
“I don’t know if I thought this news would ever come, honestly,” Ashini said.
“I’m proud to bring you this letter that our history will forever be recognized that we were here longer than 300 years … and they’re not going to erase our grandparents and they’re forever marked."
Wakeham said he hopes the province and the Innu Nation can continue to work toward reconciliation.
"It was important for me to try to mend that relationship. None of us want to be at odds, and I think for both myself and Minister [Lela] Evans, that was important."

items: A previous version of this story quoted Tony Wakeham as saying in the letter there was controversy around the "300-year theory." In fact, the letter Wakeham wrote said "300-year issue," and Ashini said "300-year theory" while reading the letter online.Nov 26, 2026 4:18 PM EST
